utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T. The Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, your full name?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: My full name is Alhaji Dimitrije Kamara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You work here in the Office of the Prosecutor as a language assistant.

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: No. I work as a translator.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Translator. Sorry. Born where?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: I was born in Belgrade, Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then I think you spent several years away and returned to Yugoslavia to complete your education when you were what age?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: When I was 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You are, therefore, fluent in what's now called B/C/S, but which can be called by various names, but it's the language of the area.

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Definitely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Working here as a translator, did you have dealings with two tapes of conversations between people on telephones?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first tape, 2801.1, produced by a witness and then to the Chamber via investigators and one of the lawyers on the team, that was originally translated by the official translation department of this institution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Subsequently, the witness produced another tape which he brought with him to the institution, 2801.4, and were you, as notified to the Chamber, sitting in court when the first track, or the first conversation of that tape was played to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as was explained to the Chamber, were you there following what you could hear on the then only official translation?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber decided that the exercise of listening to the whole of the tape was unrealistic, given the problem suffered understandably by the simultaneous translators -- interpreters, and the matter was adjourned, that further inquiries should be made; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you since then done two things in relation to these two tapes? First, did you listen to both tapes with the original translation to hand to check if the tapes were identical in content or not?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By that method, what was the result that you discovered?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: There was no doubt in my mind that both of the tapes are exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, incidentally, this morning, I hope not too late, I alerted -- probably too late, I alerted Ms. Featherstone by telephone to the desirability of bringing those earlier transcripts in with you, and I don't know if you've got them with you or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have mine, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As I recall, as I went through that tape with you, I attempted to annotate it as to where the numbered conversations began and ended, and since there's been an addition to the transcript, it may be that the Chamber would want to have the earlier versions with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kamara, did you thereafter become involved to a limited degree in the negotiations, or attempted negotiations, between the lawyers, sitting in on certainly one meeting with Mr. Stein and Mr. Lopez-Terres?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Yes, and there was also an interpreter from the Defence present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think on that occasion, you did listen -- all of you listened to all or part of one or both of the tapes?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: We did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On that occasion, were you able to hear on a tape some sounds that have been referred to as being on one tape but not on the other?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: I remember hearing a sound, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had you noticed those sounds when you had listened to either tape before?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: I had not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But following that, was it apparent to you that there was the possibility for further clarification of one passage of the tape which you judged to have been incompletely translated?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Yes, there was a portion of the tape that had not been fully transcribed. It was written as "not clear" or something like that, but there was a part that could be made out, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you then translate that additional passage of the tape?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: I did. I transcribed it into B/C/S first and then translated it into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, the Court, I hope, has the additional transcripts that were provided. And what may be helpful, it would be simply and swiftly to run through the start and the stop points of the conversations on the new version -- right. Thank you very much. The new version is 2801.A, with serial number 913915 on the first page, and if that can go to the witness. Everybody else has already had these provided. So can I hand that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. The interpreters do not have either of the versions by now. Could we please have some?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have the new version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's very much my failing. Yes. When I come to the relevant passage, I'll ask the witness to put it on the ELMO. The Chamber will recall that because of the initial interest in the very first conversation between Kordic and Blaskic, which was the first conversation transcribed, that conversation is a separate small transcription and there has been no need to change that. Therefore, we pick up on this document, 2801.A at what is and was originally notated at conversation number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that running through this latest document, for the avoidance of any doubt, if we start at the top of what is page 1 of this exhibit, Mr. Kamara, is that conversation 2, and it starts at the top of page 1 and it runs on to six lines down to page 2?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So conversation 3 begins at line 8 of page 2 and runs on to line 17 of page 3?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Yes. Line 16 of page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Line 16. So line 18 is the beginning of conversation 4. That conversation goes over to page 5, and line 1 of page 5 has the end of that conversation with Blaskic saying, "Bye," and line 3, that's the giving of conversation number 5.

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Conversation number 5 runs through to page 10, where it ends at line 14. Conversation 6, picking up at line 16.

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That conversation ends, I think, at the foot of page 10, and at the top of page 11 we have the beginning at line 2 of conversation 7.

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That ends at the foot of page 11, and conversation 8 begins at the top of page 12. Slightly ambiguous in that the very first line on page 12 says "Bye," "Hello," but in any event, there's a new conversation there.

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Conversation 8 goes on some two and a half pages to page 14, where it ends at line 8, with conversation 9 beginning at line 10.

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Conversation 10 goes on to page 18 -- it's a longer conversation -- ending at line 25.

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And conversation 10 beginning at line 17 -- 27?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Line 27, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. We're now in the territory of the passage of the tape which you found it could be better dealt with. We may not be quite there yet but we're getting there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, if we just compare -- if I just compare this. At page 18, which we're on at the moment, line 27, that's the beginning of conversation 10, and it goes over, as we see, to page 19, and to something that then says "Side B." Then from side B we go on for a little bit. Was there anything else on side A that needed adding to or is the balance of side A correct as originally --

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: The balance is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. But we can see that conversation 10 begins at line 27, and that that side of the tape ends at line 5 on page 19. Was that one conversation at that stage or more or can't you say?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: It was. It was one conversation. The line and -- it was a very poor tape. The quality was very poor, but I think I can say, yes, that it was one conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then on page 19, when we change sides, and the first thing transcribed is that, "The line is very bad," were you able to form a view on whether this was the continuation of the conversation or not?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: It was impossible to say because of the quality of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. But whatever was being said at the beginning of side B, it appeared to end at line 24?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Yes. It ended at line 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. So that what starts at line 26 is a new conversation, and depending on whether the first bit is counted as its own conversation or part of the previous conversation, then this, at line 26, is either number 1 or number 2 by way of fresh conversations on this side. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the original transcription, how much had been found of this?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: I think only four lines had been transcribed in the original transcription.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this was, on page 19 of the earlier transcription, marked as "inaudible"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you, by listening what, once or more than once?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Well, twice. The first time at the meeting with the Defence counsel and the second time by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you were able to decipher how many lines that we see on page 19 as fresh lines of transcription and translation?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: From number 7 to number 24, and from number 26 to number 7 on page 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those, therefore, reveal something of a conversation, whether from the previous side or not, from line 6 to line 24, and then from line 26, conversation 1 or 2, however we describe it, of this tape, going over to line 7 on page 20?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there then a break in the conversation so that what starts at line 9 is conversation 2 or conversation 3, however described, of that tape?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then in accordance with the earlier transcription, that conversation goes over to page 26, where we have the end of that conversation at line 6, and it picks up at line 8 with the next conversation, which can be numbered 3 or 4. That conversation goes over to page 31, where at line 32 the conversation ends, and at line 34, we have the start of what is either conversation 4 or 5. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That takes us to the end of the tape. Sorry, I said I was going to put that on the ELMO. I didn't and I should have done. This reveals, for those who also have the index on the tape box, some difficulty in understanding exactly what happens as between the end of side A and side B, the author of the index having got to 11 conversations on side A and 3 conversations on side B. Yes?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But as you've explained, save by careful listening, it plainly wasn't possible for the official translators to decipher a whole conversation although there was one there?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What you discovered by the additional careful listening, does that affect at all your decision that the two tapes are identical in content?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: No. The two tapes are identical in content.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me just object to this witness being put on because we have not had the two weeks' notice that was required by the Scheduling Order entered earlier on in this case. In fact, we've had about one day's notice. But I just want the objection to be stated for the record, I'm not going to belabour the point, and I'll do my best to cross-examine in short order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if there's any matter which you say is a cause of prejudice to you, you can draw it to our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kamara, there's no question in your mind, I take it, therefore, that there are not 11 conversations on side A of this tape, there are actually 10?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And equally, there's no question that there are not three conversations on side B of the tape, but, depending on how you count the first one, there are either four or five, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You are not a tape-quality expert or a technical expert with respect to the actual process of recordation or anything like that, technical aspects of tape-recording; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You are simply a translator. I don't mean to belittle your position, but you are a translator, a language expert, rather than a technical expert; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: I'm a translator, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And there was no question in your mind that you could see significant differences in the tape quality between the various conversations on tape side A and tape side B; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You have no explanation for the variation in that quality, do you?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you're saying, sir, that when you listened to the taped conversation that I think gave the initial translators difficulty, and forgive me while I just flip through this on my feet here, but I believe this was on page 19, is that correct, page 19 of the exhibit that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Page 19, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Side B. The original translators who heard that could not translate it, could they? They said that the tape quality was so poor that the conversation there was basically inaudible; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I would like to say that the original tape was most probably done by a language assistant, because language assistants are the ones who transcribe tapes into B/C/S, and these are translated by translators into English. And whether the tape quality was so poor or whether it was due to human error, I wouldn't be able to say at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You don't know whether it was done by a language assistant or a translator, do you?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: I can assume because, as I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you don't know, do you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But at all events, whether it was a language assistant or a translator, they were employees of the Office of the Prosecutor, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Definitely. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That needs correcting, of course. As I'm sure Mr. Sayers will recall, the interpreters who work here work for the institution as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Be careful, Mr. Sayers. You must be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I apologise for that, Your Honour. That was my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But the point is, sir, that the first translators that worked for the institution couldn't hear it, but you say you could, right, and hear it sufficiently well to be able to translate it.

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that they couldn't hear it. They might have heard it but deemed that it was of very poor quality and not of any significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only one thing arising, or two things arising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I take it you've got no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, sir, we don't. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The difference in quality, are you able to say whether that's a difference in the tape quality or a difference in the quality of the sound that was being tape-recorded?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: The difference in tape quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why do you say that? Because we have lots of references in the conversation to people saying there was a poor line, and matters of that sort.

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Yes, the line was very bad. The line itself was very bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. So what are you saying? You're not an expert, but what are you saying about the tape quality?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: It depends on the very tape -- because these tapes were recorded on maybe two different machines, or the same machine, and the head could have been dirty, or something like that, and that could have affected the quality. But that's just an assumption of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. So no expertise, an assumption. And what are you saying about the differences; within parts of each tape that there are differences or between the two tapes?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: No, there are no differences between the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Since you've been asked about the difference between language assistants and translators, what is the difference?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: The difference is translators [sic] are general staff, they are G-level staff, and translators are P-level staff, and translators go through much more rigorous testing before being employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You said translators are general staff. Did you mean --

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: Sorry. Language assistants are general staff; translators are professional staff, and they go through much more rigorous testing before being employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But the policy of the institution in relation to the transcription of tapes generally is that they are transcribed by?

utterances.speaker: ALHAJI DIMITRIJE KAMARA
utterances.text: If the tapes are in B/C/S, then they're translated by language assistants, and then translated by translators into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing else arising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kamara, thank you for coming. That concludes your evidence. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was hoping that we might next deal with the outstanding village binders. Mr. Scott and Mr. Lopez-Terres are coming down to deal with that; I hope they'd be here immediately, but that they be here any second, I'm sure. While I'm waiting for them, can I deal with a couple of administrative matters. First, and I don't mind mentioning this in the presence of the defendants, I think today is the return date for the production of materials --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- and I'm not sure how we're going to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We have it in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. There is now in place, I think, an arrangement for the taking of videolink evidence from three witnesses next Wednesday. I'm hopeful, indeed, that we can accomplish three witnesses in the single day. It may be necessary, of course, to have a full day, and one's always got to have a certain anxiety about the technical side of things going wrong, because it sometimes breaks down. Obviously, I'll be dealing with witnesses in as compact a way as I can by the production of summaries which they will acknowledge and so on. I'm asked to have in mind at least the possibility that there may be the need, for one reason or another, to extend into Thursday, when it's known that His Honour Judge Robinson wouldn't be available, and I've been asked to at least give consideration to the possibility of the Chamber, if necessary, dealing with that evidence by just two of its members, if there is an accidental spillage over. So I mention it now rather than the matter arising later. Then the only other outstanding matters until we can deal with the village witnesses and exhibits is just to notify you that in relation to the taker of the statement of the deceased witness, we've had a couple of inquiries which we've been able to respond to, and we're going to be told next week if that witness is required, and if not, she won't be called. She's only available on a couple of days next week. I think Mr. Lopez-Terres is in a position to deal with the binder of Novi Travnik, if that would be convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Excuse me. What do you mean exactly by "deal with the binder"? That means what? Because I would like to know the l'ordre du jour. The problem of dealing with the binder exactly, what are the questions concerned there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In each case, we have to be sure that there is agreement about what material is in and is not being objected to in the binder, because the binder then becomes part of the record of the hearing, that's all, and it's better for these things to be dealt with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The binders should be in court. Are they in front of us? Perhaps Judge Bennouna would like one. Mr. Lopez-Terres, let's deal with Novi Travnik. I've got the index. There's mention of a report, you haven't included that, obviously; there's the census and the videos, which have already been tendered; the statements, which presumably you're not going to try and argue should be admitted; then we come to the transcripts. Now, you'll have to help. These are the -- I'm looking at number 5, transcripts, these are the Kordic witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So they won't be in the binder, presumably.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's an inventory of all the exhibits referring to the facts committed in the municipality of Novi Travnik, including exhibits concerning our case and which are only there as a reminder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Then turning to the exhibits, most have already been tendered --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the category, paragraph 6, maps, there is Exhibit 1960 and 1962, which, until now, have not been presented to your Chamber, and they do not appear to us to be indispensable, in view of the large number of maps that we have seen, to tender these new maps. They are there simply as part of the inventory because we have tried to be as exhaustive as possible and to identify all those documents. As regards the maps, I think that the Office of the Prosecutor is no longer going to request that they be admitted. On the other hand, regarding Category 7, there are several documents which have still not been admitted. There is 7.1, 7.2. Regarding 7.2, we have the first order, signed by Anto Valenta. We have had no reaction of the Defence regarding their position on this document. The same applies to document 137 a little further on in this paragraph, an ECMM report.
